newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian dlr under a cloud, mixed data no help.
newsitem.headline: Australian dlr under a cloud, mixed data no help.

text.p: The Australian dollar was struggling at the midsession as a modest offshore bounce ran into U.S. fund sales at the first chart hurdle of US$0.7675.

Traders said it found interim support at US$0.7650 and there was enough talk of bids, including rumours of options-related orders, around US$0.7635 to cushion the currency for the moment. They also reckoned the market was still short after Friday's tumble, offering at least the scope for a squeeze this week.
Today's domestic data on business investment were stronger than expected for the first quarter just gone, but showed some worrying slippage in forward spending estimates for 1997/98.
By 12.15 pm (0215 GMT) the dollar had edged back to US$0.7658/63 having drifted up to US$0.7672/77 at the opening from a US$0.7635 low offshore.
It had ended Monday here at US$0.7662/67 and trading overseas had been less than meaningful with both the U.K. and U.S. off on holiday.

Chart watchers said there was a still a chance of a short covering rise to the US$0.7710/20 area which marked the floor of the dollar's range for six weeks before Friday's 1-1/2 cent dive. But most recommended selling at those level if seen for an eventual re-test of US$0.7635 and retracement to US$0.7550.
On the crosses the currency had trailed off to 88.96/06 yen from an early 89.46 high, but was steady on Monday's late 88.80/90.
The yen found support from rising Japanese bond yields with heavy options-related selling saw the 10-year JGB benchmark jump to a 1997 high of 2.645 percent from a previous 2.580.

That helped the yen recoup some ground from the mark, which itself had benefited from safe haven flows Monday following the surprising strength of the left wing parties in the first round of the French general election on Sunday. The A$ was just a spectator to all this and tended to take its cue from US$ moves.
In trade weighted terms the local dollar firmed slightly to 58.3 from a previous 58.0 close, but again well short of the 59.1 level held before Friday's rate cut.
The Reserve Bank's surprise move had greatly reduced the relevance of this week's helping of domestic economic data which were mostly too dated to say anything new about policy.

Thus the 6.5 percent rise in private capital expenditure for the March quarter had scant market impact even though it easily beat forecasts of a 3.5 percent gain. The jump in spending also promised to contribute a little more to GDP growth in the quarter than previously thought.
But analysts felt that what happened back in Q1 was almost irrelevant given the RBA had felt it necessary to cut rates now, half way through the year.
Indeed, the bank's readiness to go for growth meant it might yet ease again if the economy fell short of expectations, and in this regard the CAPEX data actually sounded a warning note.

This came from a survey of estimated investment expenditure for 1997/98 which showed growth in spending expectations was not nearly as strong as this time last year. The Bureau of Statistics holds seven surveys in all, starting three quarters before the financial year in question.
Today's March quarter data included the second estimate for for 1997/98 which, at A$36.57 billion, was 14.7 percent up on the first estimate taken in the December quarter.

However, the gain was exaggerated because the first estimate was revised down to A$31.90 billion from an intitial A$34.68 billion. Compared to corresponding estimate for 1996/97 the second estimate was only 1.5 percent higher.

And, crucially, the second estimate for 1996/97 had been a whopping 22.7 percent above that of the previous year, a result which contributed greatly to expectations of strong business investment growth for the current financial year.

Analaysts said the data suggested business investment would come close to the government's budget forecast of 16 percent business investment growth in 1996/97, but would fall short of its 1997/98 forecast of eight percent growth.
Last week's rate cut, therefore, could prove to be a timely development if it bolstered business investment plans for the year ahead.

Also out this week are business inventories and the balance of payments for Q1, and data on retail trade, the goods and services trade balance and motor vehicle registrations for April. -- Wayne Cole 61-2 9373 1800
